questions.prompt: Under a microscope, an amoeba stretches around a smaller single-celled organism and swallows it whole. What makes the amoeba a consumer?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Under a microscope, an amoeba stretches around a smaller single-celled organism and swallows it whole. What makes the amoeba a consumer?

choices.text: It gets food from another organism
choices.rationale: Correct. A consumer can't make its own food, so it gets matter and energy from other organisms. Engulfing prey is exactly that.

choices.text: It is made of only one cell
choices.rationale: Cell count doesn't decide the role. Some single-celled organisms, such as many algae, make their own food by photosynthesis and are producers.

choices.text: It carries out cellular respiration
choices.rationale: Producers carry out cellular respiration too, so respiration can't be what separates a consumer from a producer.

choices.text: It moves around on its own
choices.rationale: Moving isn't the test. Some single-celled algae swim with tiny tails yet make their own food. What matters is where the food comes from.

questions.explanation: A consumer is any organism that can't make its own food and instead gets matter and energy from other organisms, by eating or absorbing them. questions.misconception: Only animals are consumers, or carrying out cellular respiration is what makes something a consumer.
questions.hint: Ask where the amoeba's food comes from.

questions.prompt: In cellular respiration, C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy. Where do the 12 hydrogen atoms from one sugar molecule end up?
questions.accessiblePrompt: The cellular respiration equation is: one C six H twelve O six, a sugar molecule with six carbon, twelve hydrogen and six oxygen atoms, plus six O two, six oxygen molecules with two oxygen atoms each, yields six C O two, six carbon dioxide molecules with one carbon and two oxygen atoms each, plus six H two O, six water molecules with two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom each, plus energy. Where do the 12 hydrogen atoms from one sugar molecule end up?

choices.text: In the six water molecules, two in each
choices.rationale: Correct. Water is the only product that contains hydrogen. Six H₂O molecules hold 6 × 2 = 12 hydrogen atoms, exactly the number the sugar brought in.

choices.text: In the six carbon dioxide molecules
choices.rationale: Carbon dioxide, CO₂, is made only of carbon and oxygen atoms, so it can't hold any of the hydrogen.

choices.text: They escape from the cell as hydrogen gas
choices.rationale: No hydrogen gas appears among the products. Every hydrogen atom is accounted for in the water.

choices.text: Back in a new sugar molecule
choices.rationale: Cellular respiration breaks sugar down; it doesn't build new sugar. Building sugar from carbon dioxide and water is photosynthesis.

questions.explanation: Atoms aren't created or destroyed, so all 12 hydrogen atoms from the sugar must show up among the products. Carbon dioxide has no hydrogen, so they all end up in water: 6 water molecules × 2 hydrogen atoms = 12. Tracing one element at a time like this is how the equation keeps track of matter.
questions.misconception: Atoms from the sugar can vanish or land in any product, instead of being counted in the product molecules that actually contain that element.
questions.hint: Check which product molecules contain any hydrogen at all.
